name: Hungary

facts.religion: Catholic about 30%, Calvinist about 10%, many unaffiliated

snapshot: Péter Magyar's Tisza party ended Viktor Orbán's 16-year rule in April 2026 with the biggest majority in Hungary's post-communist history.
culture: Hungarian is not related to its neighbours' languages, and that isolation has shaped a strong national identity. Budapest's thermal baths, Liszt and Bartók, goulash and paprika are famous exports. The memory of the 1920 Treaty of Trianon, which cost Hungary two-thirds of its territory, still resonates, as does the 1956 uprising against Soviet rule.
society: Under Orbán, Hungary became the EU's model of "illiberal democracy", with friendly oligarchs owning most media and billions in EU funds frozen over rule-of-law concerns. Magyar, a former Fidesz insider, has promised to unlock those funds and fight corruption. Hungary has an ageing population and low wages by EU standards.
situation: For 16 years Viktor Orbán ran Hungary as the EU's self-declared "illiberal democracy": he rewrote the constitution, redrew electoral maps, filled courts with loyalists and turned state television into a party outlet, while blocking EU policy on Ukraine and cultivating Putin and Trump. Many people believed he had rigged the system so thoroughly that he could not lose. On 12 April, he lost in a landslide.

Péter Magyar, a former Fidesz insider who broke with Orbán in 2024, led his new Tisza party to 141 of 199 seats, the largest majority in Hungary's post-communist history, while Fidesz fell from 135 to 52 (AP via KTLA). Orbán conceded on election night. Magyar was sworn in on 9 May promising to "serve, not rule" and a "change of system" (The Star). With a two-thirds supermajority, he can now rewrite Orbán's constitution. He suspended the news programming of the state broadcaster, which had served Fidesz for years, until it could be independent, created separate ministries for health, education and environment, and set out to unlock about €17 billion in EU funds frozen over rule-of-law concerns. Critics pounced when his brother-in-law was named justice minister. His first real crisis was a record heatwave and drought. He has said Hungary still needs Russian oil and gas in the short term. Orbán's defeat removed the EU's biggest internal obstacle and the model that populists across Europe had studied.
power: A parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the majority in the 199-seat National Assembly, elected by a mixed system; a two-thirds majority can change the constitution and "cardinal laws." The president, elected by parliament, is largely ceremonial.
holders: Prime Minister Péter Magyar (Tisza), in office since 9 May 2026.
